result: Bioinformatics analysis identified approximately 100 transmembrane proteins containing a GXXXN motif in their first transmembrane helix, most of which are GPCRs, including 13 of 16 known CC and CXC chemokine receptors.
evaluation: Claims C20, C21, C80, and C93 are supported by the bioinformatics analysis presented in Table 1 and Table 1—source data 1. The methodology is described in the Materials and Methods section, and the results are clearly documented. This provides a solid foundation for the subsequent experimental work on CCR5.

result: C6-ceramide treatment increases cell-surface accessibility of C-terminally tagged CCR5 and other GXXXN motif-containing GPCRs (CCR1, CCR4, CCR10, MAS1) by 10- to 150-fold, but not β2AR which lacks the motif, suggesting topology inversion that brings the C-terminus to the extracellular space.
evaluation: Claims C24, C26, C27, and C28 are well-supported by the SNAP-tag fluorescent labeling data in Figure 1B. The experimental design appropriately uses cell-impermeable and cell-permeable reagents to distinguish topology, includes a negative control (β2AR), and shows specificity for GXXXN motif-containing receptors. The quantitative data with error bars support the magnitude of the effect.

result: Immunofluorescence microscopy demonstrates that the C-terminal Myc-tag of CCR5 is undetectable without permeabilization in untreated cells but becomes visible on the cell surface after ceramide treatment, while CCR5 is detectable regardless of ceramide treatment when cells are permeabilized.
evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 1C-F and the control experiment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The experimental design properly controls for cell permeabilization artifacts by testing Giantin detection. The results are consistent with topology inversion bringing the C-terminus extracellularly.

result: Ceramide treatment produces a lower molecular weight form of CCR5 consistent with loss of O-linked glycosylation, as demonstrated by immunoblot analysis showing time-dependent appearance of the lower MW band and by glycosylation-site mutants that migrate at the same MW regardless of ceramide treatment.
evaluation: Claims C35, C36, C38, and C88 are supported by immunoblot data in Figures 2B and 2C. The experimental logic is sound: if topology inversion places the N-terminus (containing all glycosylation sites) in the cytosol, glycosylation should not occur. The glycosylation mutant control (C38) provides strong supporting evidence. However, the authors acknowledge alternative interpretations in the Discussion.

result: N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5 shows reduced cell-surface labeling by cell-impermeable reagent after ceramide treatment, consistent with N-terminus moving from extracellular to cytosolic location, and this effect is not due to reduced protein expression.
evaluation: Claims C37, C40, and C41 are supported by data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2. The N-terminal tagging approach provides complementary evidence to the C-terminal tagging experiments. The control showing no change in total protein expression (C41) rules out a trivial explanation. The fact that the construct contains a signal peptide yet still undergoes RAT (C42, C87) is noted.

result: Cell-surface biotin labeling of cysteine residues demonstrates that a CCR5 topology reporter (with only extracellular cysteines in the A form) is biotinylated and precipitated in untreated cells but not after ceramide treatment, while wildtype CCR5 (with cysteines on both sides) is precipitated regardless of treatment, confirming that inverted CCR5(B) reaches the cell surface.
evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by the biotin labeling data in Figures 2E-G. The experimental design is clever: the topology reporter allows discrimination between A and B forms based on cysteine accessibility. The wildtype control (C45) demonstrates that ceramide does not simply cause internalization. This provides strong evidence for topology inversion with cell surface localization.

result: LPS treatment of mouse peritoneal macrophages increases production of dihydroceramide (but not ceramide) as measured by LC-MS, with specific increases in multiple dihydroceramide species.
evaluation: Claims C48 and C5 are supported by LC-MS data in Figure 3A. The quantitative measurements show statistically significant increases in dihydroceramide species upon LPS treatment. The observation that dihydroceramide rather than ceramide is produced differs from prior reports in RAW264.7 cells (C47), which the authors appropriately note. The data are clear and well-controlled.

result: LPS treatment prevents detection of CCR5 by an antibody against the second extracellular loop in non-permeabilized macrophages, but CCR5 remains detectable in permeabilized cells; this effect is reversed by FB1, which blocks dihydroceramide synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C50, C51, C52, and C54 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figures 3B-I and LC-MS data in Figure 3A. The experimental design properly controls for permeabilization and uses FB1 to establish the causal link between dihydroceramide production and topology inversion. The antibody specificity is confirmed in Ccr5-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

result: Immuno-gold electron microscopy demonstrates that CCR5-specific gold particle clusters are located on the extracellular side of plasma membranes in untreated macrophages but on the intracellular side (not in endocytic vesicles) after LPS treatment, with quantification showing the vast majority of labeled CCR5 undergoes this topological switch.
evaluation: Claims C55, C56, C57, and C6 are supported by immuno-gold EM data in Figures 3J-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 3. This provides direct ultrastructural evidence for topology inversion at the plasma membrane. The quantification (C57, ~20 cells per condition) and the exclusion of endocytic vesicles (C56) strengthen the conclusion. The authors appropriately note that only gold clusters (not single particles) were counted to ensure specificity.

result: In vivo LPS administration (intraperitoneal injection) induces CCR5 topology inversion in isolated macrophages, and this effect is blocked by co-injection of FB1.
evaluation: Claims C58 and C59 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A-L. This in vivo experiment addresses potential artifacts of in vitro LPS treatment and demonstrates physiological relevance. The FB1 rescue experiment establishes the mechanistic link to dihydroceramide synthesis in vivo. The experimental design is appropriate.

result: LPS treatment completely blocks CCR5-dependent migration of macrophages toward the chemokine ligand CCL5, as demonstrated by transwell migration assays showing migration in wildtype but not Ccr5-/- macrophages, and complete inhibition by LPS in wildtype cells.
evaluation: Claims C61, C63, and C7 are supported by migration assay data in Figure 5A. The use of Ccr5-/- macrophages as a control (C63) demonstrates that the migration is CCR5-dependent. The complete blockade by LPS is consistent with topology inversion preventing ligand binding. The functional consequence of topology inversion is clearly demonstrated.

result: FB1 co-treatment eliminates the inhibitory effect of LPS on macrophage migration toward CCL5, demonstrating that LPS blocks chemotaxis by inducing CCR5 topology inversion through dihydroceramide synthesis.
evaluation: Claims C64, C78, and C79 are supported by migration assay data in Figure 5B. This rescue experiment establishes the causal chain: LPS → dihydroceramide → topology inversion → loss of chemotaxis. The experimental logic is sound and the data are consistent with the model. This represents a key mechanistic link in the paper.

result: The authors conclude that ceramide or related sphingolipids can invert the topology of GPCRs containing a GXXXN motif, that GPCRs may not always adopt the same topology, that membrane proteins can be regulated by topological inversion through RAT, and that the GXXXN motif may be a previously unrecognized mechanism for proper GPCR insertion and regulation.
evaluation: Claims C3, C8, C91, C95, and C96 represent the main conclusions of the paper. These are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches (SNAP-tag labeling, immunofluorescence, glycosylation analysis, biotin labeling, EM, and functional assays) across both cell culture and in vivo systems. The conclusions are appropriately stated as possibilities (C3, C95, C96) given that only CCR5 was extensively characterized, though multiple GPCRs showed similar responses to ceramide.

result: The authors infer that CXCR4 and other CC/CXC chemokine receptors containing the GXXXN motif are likely subjected to topological regulation through RAT, and that LPS may invert the topology of all these receptors.
evaluation: Claims C73 and C81 are speculative extrapolations from the CCR5 data. While the bioinformatics analysis shows these receptors contain the GXXXN motif, and limited data show ceramide effects on CCR1, CCR4, CCR10 (C26), direct experimental evidence for topology inversion of CXCR4 and comprehensive testing of all CC/CXC receptors is lacking. The inference is reasonable but requires experimental validation.

result: The authors propose a model where unprimed macrophages migrate toward CCL5 via CCR5(A), but upon encountering LPS, dihydroceramide production triggers RAT to produce CCR5(B), blocking further migration and potentially explaining reduced chemotaxis in sepsis.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 represent a speculative but well-supported model integrating the experimental findings. The model is consistent with all the data presented (dihydroceramide production, topology inversion, loss of chemotaxis, FB1 rescue). The connection to sepsis (C69) is appropriately presented as speculative and supported by citation (C70). The model provides a coherent biological interpretation of the findings.

result: The authors speculate that topological inversion of CCR5 and CXCR4 should block HIV entry by making viral binding sites inaccessible, consistent with prior reports that ceramide-increasing treatments confer HIV resistance, and suggest that compounds inducing RAT without LPS toxicity might be effective anti-HIV therapeutics.
evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are speculative. While the logic is sound (if N-terminus and second extracellular loop are intracellular, HIV cannot bind), no direct HIV entry experiments are presented. The consistency with prior literature (C76) is supportive but not definitive. The therapeutic speculation (C77) is premature without experimental validation. This represents an interesting hypothesis for future work but is not experimentally supported in this manuscript.

result: The authors acknowledge that CCR5 can be desensitized through arrestin-mediated internalization and state it remains unclear whether topological inversion through RAT is the only mechanism by which LPS inhibits CCR5 activity.
evaluation: Claims C84 and C85 appropriately acknowledge limitations in the interpretation. While the data strongly support topology inversion as a mechanism, the authors correctly note that other desensitization mechanisms exist and their relative contributions are unclear. This represents appropriate scientific caution and identifies an area for future investigation.

result: The authors report that the N48L mutation in CCR5 (intended to lock topology) resulted in ER retention rather than cell surface expression, and acknowledge they cannot rule out that this mutation affects protein folding, making it unsuitable for studying inverted CCR5 function.
evaluation: Claims C100 and C101 describe a negative result and appropriate interpretation. The authors attempted to create a constitutively inverted CCR5 mutant but the protein was retained in the ER. They appropriately acknowledge this limitation and do not overinterpret the result. This represents good scientific practice in reporting unsuccessful experiments and their limitations.

result: The manuscript includes extensive background information and citations to prior work on GPCR structure, topology determination mechanisms, TM4SF20 RAT, chemokine receptor function, HIV co-receptors, and related topics.
evaluation: These claims (C1, C2, C9-C19, C22, C23, C25, C33, C34, C39, C42, C47, C49, C53, C60, C62, C65, C70, C71, C74, C82, C83, C86, C89, C92, C94, C98, C99) represent background knowledge and prior work appropriately cited throughout the manuscript. They provide context for the current study and are generally well-supported by the cited literature. These are not novel findings of this study but establish the foundation for the work.

result: The authors note that N-terminally SNAP-tagged CCR5 (containing a CD8 signal peptide) still undergoes ceramide-induced RAT, and that significant amounts of CCR5 in ceramide or LPS-treated cells are localized on the cell surface.
evaluation: Claims C87 and C90 are supported by the experimental data (Figures 2D, 2F-G, and immunofluorescence/EM data). These observations are important for ruling out alternative interpretations: C87 shows that signal peptides don't prevent RAT (consistent with prior TM4SF20 work), and C90 argues against ER retention as an alternative explanation. Both strengthen the topology inversion model.

result: The authors speculate that topological inversion not only inhibits GPCR functions but also simultaneously activates functions performed by the protein with the inverted topology.
evaluation: Claim C97 is purely speculative. While the authors cite examples of inverted seven-transmembrane proteins with non-GPCR functions (C98, C99), no experiments in this manuscript address what functions inverted CCR5 or other GPCRs might have. The authors acknowledge in the Discussion that they lack suitable tools to study inverted CCR5 function (C100, C101). This represents an interesting hypothesis but is entirely unsupported by experimental data.
